claims.claim: Walton criticises A Song for Arbonne as too slight, too conventional and too distanced to carry its own weight.
claims.quote: too slight, too conventional, and too distanced

claims.feature: other: magic quantity across the oeuvre
claims.claim: Walton describes a trajectory away from magic across Kay's books, with Fionavar full of magic, Tigana less, Arbonne less again, and The Lions of Al-Rassan containing nothing but an accurate prophecy.
Kate Nepveu writes that Sailing to Sarantium shows its major plot events through multiple points of view, some dominant and accented by many minor ones.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'Review: Sailing to Sarantium', steelypips.org, 12 May 1999 (originally posted to rec.arts.sf.written)
claims.quote: shown through multiple points of view, where some dominate but
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'However, Crispin is not the sole focus'

claims.claim: Nepveu writes that Kay's mosaic technique rewards careful reading because small details relayed in one area refer to and reflect larger ones elsewhere.
claims.quote: small details relayed in one area refer to and reflect
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'However, Crispin is not the sole focus'

claims.claim: Nepveu identifies a throw-away line in the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium, a sandalmaker's having seen a ghost, as the first signal that the book is not a straight historical.
claims.quote: a throw-away line in the prologue is the first signal

claims.claim: The Speculiction reviewer identifies as a habit of Kay's middle period numerous throwaway lines that flash forward to a later consequence.
claims.source: Jesse, 'Review of Sailing to Sarantium by Guy Gavriel Kay', Speculiction, 6 May 2014
claims.quote: there are numerous throwaway lines to the effect
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Forever utilizing the patient voice'

claims.claim: The Speculiction reviewer says these flash-forward throwaway lines are fewer in Sailing to Sarantium than in A Song for Arbonne and all but dry up once Crispin reaches Sarantium.
claims.quote: by the time Crispin arrives in Sarantium they all but dry up
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Forever utilizing the patient voice'

claims.claim: The Speculiction reviewer calls Kay's the patient voice of the storyteller, skipping ahead, back and around to provide a variety of entry points into each scene.
claims.quote: the patient voice of the storyteller
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Forever utilizing the patient voice'

claims.claim: Joshua Palmatier writes that Tigana taught him fantasy works because the majority of the world it is set in is contrasted against a backdrop essentially ninety per cent familiar.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier, 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Tor.com, 6 July 2016
claims.quote: a backdrop that was essentially 90 percent familiar

claims.claim: Palmatier writes that Kay alters the familiar through all aspects of life, down to arbitrary everyday rituals, including myths, legends and superstitions.
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'How he does is it arcane'

claims.claim: Palmatier says the flavour of Italy in Tigana is carried in the word structure, the place names, the characters, the gestures and the traditions rather than in the map.
claims.quote: in the word structure, the place names, the characters

claims.feature: other: two moons and cosmetic markers
claims.claim: Palmatier calls devices such as two moons or a changed landscape mere cosmetic changes, and locates Kay's craft in subtler alterations.
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'How he does is it arcane'

claims.claim: Palmatier says that for him the true art of Kay's work is not in the use of language but in the subtle skewing of a familiar setting.
claims.quote: is not in the use of language

claims.claim: Bill Capossere describes a move between micro and macro in Written on the Dark: a tight third-person point of view for most of the story, zooming outward at times via an omniscient narrator far less bound by space or time.
claims.source: Bill Capossere, review of Written on the Dark, FantasyLiterature.com, May 2025
claims.quote: zoom outward via an omniscient narrator far less bound by

claims.claim: Capossere identifies a mode in which the zoom-out pulls way back to show a more general impact on the world, such as the Asharites' first intent to conquer Sarantium.
claims.quote: to pull way, way back and show a more general impact
